messages.author: 754d9cdc8c4dfb07
messages.subject: sem results interpretation
parts:
I considered two different model:
    1. exogenous variables: A, B, C, D;    endogenous variable: F
    2. exogenous variables: A, B, C, E;    endogenous variable: F
Both model pass test statistic:

Model 1:
lavaan 0.6-6 ended normally after 102 iterations

  Estimator                                         ML
  Optimization method                           NLMINB
  Number of free parameters                         14
                                                      
  Number of observations                           712
                                                      
Model Test User Model:
                                                      
  Test statistic                                 2.389
  Degrees of freedom                                 1
  P-value (Chi-square)                           0.122


Model 2:
lavaan 0.6-6 ended normally after 100 iterations

  Estimator                                         ML
  Optimization method                           NLMINB
  Number of free parameters                         14
                                                      
  Number of observations                           712
                                                      
Model Test User Model:
                                                      
  Test statistic                                 0.150
  Degrees of freedom                                 1
  P-value (Chi-square)                           0.699



But the Rsquare statistic works at the opposite: 
Model 1 Rsquare: 0.922 
Model 2 Rsquare: 0.849


Can anyone explain me this results?
Maybe because endogenous variable is not normally distributed?


Thank you!

messages.author: 12fdd832cacb825e
messages.subject: Re: sem results interpretation
parts:
Alessandro,

The two models have different predictors. The R^2 is going to be
different, because D and E don't have exactly the same relations to F
(and the other predictors). I'm not sure why this is surprising.

Pat

In addition to Pat. The first (chi-square test) is an overidentification test and assesses how well the model and the data fit together. The other (R^2) is an indicator of prognosis quality. There is no reason to assume that both have to point in the same direction.

Adding to this, it's often harder to get a model that fits well that
has higher correlations among the observed variables (and usually
therefore a higher R^2). So what seems paradoxical is actually fairly
common.
